# Shaken butter

Cream shaken in a jar, passed hand to hand, until it turns to butter and buttermilk.

## Ingredients

- 1 cup heavy cream
- a pinch of salt

## Tools

- a jar with a tight lid
- a bowl of cold water
- a spoon

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Pour the cream into the jar and close the lid tight.
- Take turns shaking. First it turns thick, then it goes quiet, then it thumps as butter forms.
- Pour off the buttermilk to taste or to save for pancakes.
- Rinse the butter in the cold water and press it with the spoon.
- Stir in the salt.
- Keep it in the refrigerator.

## Why we use it

Children feel and hear the cream change in their own hands as they share the work.

## I wonder

- I wonder what is making the thumping sound inside the jar.
- I wonder where the buttermilk came from.

## Connections

- Pancakes, made with the buttermilk.
- Whole wheat bread and garlic toast, to spread it on.
- All year, in every class.

## Clean up

- Jar, bowl and spoon. Rinsed in hot water first to melt the butter, then washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.
- The educator wipes the table and checks each tool before it is put away.

# Scrambled eggs

Eggs children crack and whisk themselves, cooked slowly on low heat.

## Ingredients

- 6 eggs
- a splash of milk
- 1 tablespoon butter

## Tools

- small cups for cracking
- a bowl and a whisk
- a pan and a spatula

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Crack each egg into a small cup first, then pour it into the bowl.
- Wash our hands again after touching raw egg.
- Whisk in the milk.
- An adult melts the butter and cooks the eggs on low heat, stirring, until no runny egg is left.

## Why we use it

Children watch a liquid turn solid with heat, and the eggs from our chickens become food we made.

## I wonder

- I wonder why the eggs turn from runny to soft and firm.
- I wonder why the shells are different colors.

## Connections

- Our chickens, and the eggs gathered with them.
- Spring, when the hens lay the most.

## Clean up

- The shells go in the trash.
- Cups, bowl and whisk. Washed in hot soapy water and dried, since they touched raw egg.
- Pan and spatula. Cooled, then washed and dried by the educator.
- The educator wipes the table with hot soapy water and checks each tool before it is put away.

# Vegetable broth from scraps

Peels and ends saved through the week, simmered into broth for our soups.

## Ingredients

- 4 cups vegetable scraps, such as onion skins, carrot peels, celery ends and herb stems
- 10 cups water

## Tools

- a freezer bag for saving scraps
- a soup pot
- a strainer

## Steps

- Save clean scraps in the freezer bag through the week.
- Leave out cabbage, broccoli and kale scraps, which make the broth bitter.
- An adult covers the scraps with the water and simmers them for one hour.
- Let it cool, then strain it.
- The cooked scraps go to the compost.

## Why we use it

Children see the parts we used to throw away become food, then go back to the garden.

## I wonder

- I wonder where the color in the broth came from.
- I wonder what the broth will taste like.

## Connections

- Minestrone soup, lentil soup and potato leek soup, made with this broth.
- Our compost, where the cooked scraps go.
- All year.

## Clean up

- Cooked scraps go to the compost.
- Soup pot and strainer. Cooled, washed and dried by the educator.
- Broth goes into closed containers in the refrigerator, labeled with the day it was made.

# Guacamole

Ripe avocados scooped and mashed by children, with lime and cilantro from our garden.

## Ingredients

- 3 ripe avocados
- 1 lime
- a pinch of salt
- a small handful of cilantro

## Tools

- a bowl
- spoons
- a fork or potato masher
- a citrus squeezer

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- An adult halves the avocados and takes out the pits.
- Scoop the avocado into the bowl.
- Mash it with the fork or masher.
- Squeeze in the lime.
- Tear in the cilantro and add the salt.

## Why we use it

Children feel a firm fruit become soft and smooth in their hands.

## I wonder

- I wonder why guacamole turns brown when it sits out.
- I wonder if the pit could grow into a tree.

## Connections

- Cilantro from our garden.
- Tortillas and tempeh tacos, to eat it with.
- Fall, when cilantro grows again in the cool weather.

## Cutting for our youngest

- Adults halve the avocados and take out the pits. Children scoop and mash.

## Clean up

- Avocado skins and lime peels go to the compost.
- Bowl, spoons, masher and squeezer. Washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.
- The educator wipes the table and checks each tool before it is put away.

# Roasted vegetables

Garden vegetables cut, tossed with oil by hand and roasted until sweet and golden.

## Ingredients

- 6 cups vegetables from the garden or the bin, such as carrots, squash, beets and potatoes
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- a pinch of salt

## Tools

- vegetable scrubbers
- cutting boards and child knives
- a large bowl
- a baking sheet

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Scrub the vegetables.
- An adult cuts hard vegetables into sticks.
- Cut the sticks into pieces with child knives.
- Toss the pieces with the oil and salt by hand in the bowl.
- Spread them on the baking sheet.
- An adult roasts them at 425 degrees for 25 to 35 minutes, turning them once.

## Why we use it

Children taste how the oven changes a vegetable they already know.

## I wonder

- I wonder why the edges turned brown and sweet.
- I wonder which vegetable will be softest.

## Connections

- The beds where the carrots, beets and squash grew.
- Peels and ends saved for vegetable broth from scraps.
- Fall and winter.

## Cutting for our youngest

- An adult cuts hard vegetables into sticks first, so each piece lies flat on the board. Children cut the sticks with child knives, using the bridge grip.
- An adult stays close beside each child who is cutting (close supervision).

## Clean up

- Child knives. Washed one at a time, never left in a sink of water, dried and returned to the knife roll with the blades covered.
- Cutting boards, bowl and scrubbers. Washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.
- Baking sheet. Cooled, then washed and dried by the educator.

# Baked sweet potatoes

Whole sweet potatoes, scrubbed and baked soft.

## Ingredients

- sweet potatoes, one for every two children

## Tools

- vegetable scrubbers
- forks
- a baking sheet

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Scrub the sweet potatoes in a basin of water.
- Prick each one with a fork.
- An adult bakes them at 400 degrees for 45 to 60 minutes, until soft.
- Let them cool, then scoop.

## Why we use it

The work is simple enough for our youngest children to do from start to finish.

## I wonder

- I wonder why the inside turned orange and soft.
- I wonder why we prick holes in the skin.

## Connections

- Fall and winter.

## Clean up

- Skins go to the compost.
- Scrubbers. Rinsed, shaken out and hung to dry.
- Forks and baking sheet. Washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help with the forks.

# Overnight oats

Oats stirred into milk and yogurt in the afternoon, soft and ready by morning.

## Ingredients

- 1 cup rolled oats
- 1 cup milk
- ½ cup yogurt
- chopped fruit from our orchard

## Tools

- a large jar
- a spoon

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Stir the oats, milk and yogurt in the jar.
- Look at how dry the oats are now.
- Refrigerate it overnight.
- In the morning, look again, then stir in the fruit.

## Why we use it

Children watch a change that happens overnight, and our own yogurt goes in.

## I wonder

- I wonder where the milk went overnight.

## Connections

- Yogurt, made by us.
- Fruit from our orchard in its season.

## Clean up

- Jar and spoon. Washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.

# Kale chips

Garden kale torn by hand and dried crisp in our dehydrator.

## Ingredients

- 1 bunch kale from our garden
- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- a pinch of salt

## Tools

- a large bowl
- the dehydrator

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Strip the leaves from the stems.
- Tear the leaves into pieces about the size of a child's palm.
- Rub in the oil and salt by hand.
- Lay the pieces flat on the dehydrator trays.
- An adult dries them at 125 degrees for 4 to 6 hours, until crisp.

## Why we use it

Children tear, rub and taste one leaf from the garden to the tray to the plate.

## I wonder

- I wonder where the water in the leaves went.
- I wonder why the chips crunch.

## Connections

- The kale and collards in our beds.
- Fruit leather and dried fruit, made in the same dehydrator.
- Fall, winter and spring.

## Clean up

- Stems go to the compost.
- Bowl. Washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.
- Dehydrator trays. Washed and air dried.

# Steamed rice

Rice rinsed until the water runs clear, then simmered soft.

## Ingredients

- 2 cups white rice
- 3 cups water

## Tools

- a strainer and a bowl
- a pot with a lid

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Rinse the rice in the bowl, pour off the cloudy water and rinse again until it runs clear.
- An adult brings the rice and water to a boil, then covers the pot and simmers it on low for 18 minutes.
- Let it rest, covered, for 10 minutes.

## Why we use it

Children watch the rinse water change from cloudy to clear, and see how much the rice grows.

## I wonder

- I wonder what makes the water cloudy.
- I wonder how much bigger the rice will grow.

## Connections

- Bean and rice bowls.
- The cloudy rinse water goes on a garden bed.
- All year.

## Clean up

- Rinse water goes on a garden bed.
- Strainer and bowl. Washed and dried. Children may help.
- Pot. Soaked, then washed and dried by the educator.
